characteristics: Modernist rationalism: mathematical modular grid, asymmetric layout, objective tone. Flat color, sans-serif only, photography over illustration. Direct precursor to flat design.
dos: Build on a strict modular grid (quadrant or column); set text flush-left ragged-right; use one sans-serif family (Helvetica/Akzidenz lineage) in few weights; crop photography to fill grid modules by 30-40%; keep palette minimal and flat.
donts: No drop shadows, no gradients, no decorative type, no ornament. Avoid for playful or emotional brands — pure rationalism reads cold in consumer-warmth contexts.

characteristics: Frosted-glass panels create openness and spatial depth without losing background context. Lineage: Vista Aero to Apple Liquid Glass.
dos: Use translucent fills (~12% white) with backdrop blur 8-20px plus saturation boost; add a 1px white ~25% border to sell the glass edge; radius ~16px; soft wide shadow (0 8px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.25)); place only over busy or colorful backgrounds.
donts: Don't use blur below 10px (reads as a rendering bug); don't place glass over flat plain backgrounds; don't skip contrast testing — text on glass must pass WCAG against the busiest expected background; avoid on data-dense UI and low-power devices (GPU cost).

characteristics: Visual rebellion against sterile templates: raw borders, hard shadows, loud accents, oversized type. Performance-friendly and focus-state clear when done right.
dos: Use 2-4px solid black borders; hard offset shadows with zero blur scaled to component size (3px badges, 5px cards, 8px overlays, 12px dialogs; format Xpx Xpx 0 0 #000); square corners; 1-3 saturated pop accents over black plus off-white base; oversized display type (personality) with plain body type; hover grows the shadow, press collapses it.
donts: Don't add blur or gradients; don't rely on color alone for states (WCAG 1.4.1); don't assume thick borders enlarge touch targets — verify hit areas; avoid for banking, healthcare, government, and dense dashboards. Body text contrast still >= 4.5:1.

characteristics: Flat geometric vector figures: tiny heads, elongated limbs (>= 1.5x torso), non-representational skin tones, no facial detail, no shadows or gradients. SVG-friendly and cheap to template.
dos: Use only if a deliberately generic, globally neutral illustration language is required and the brand carries no trust-critical stakes; build characters from primitives; keep it resolution-independent SVG. Card chrome: flat white or single-pastel surface, no shadows or gradients, radius 8-12px.
donts: By 2025-2026 this style reads dated and generic-corporate; critics associate it with 'toxic positivity' masking real product friction. Flag it in design reviews rather than recommending it; never use for brands positioning on trust, craft, or seriousness.

characteristics: Techno-utopian optimism: cool blues and greens, glossy translucency, nature motifs (bubbles, water, leaves, clouds) fused with digital sheen. Gen-Z nostalgia revival is current.
dos: Create depth with glossy specular highlights and reflective 'wet' sheen rather than drop shadows; use translucent panes; pair vibrant blue-green palettes with white; simplified nature iconography for freshness and optimism. Card chrome: glossy translucent panel (white 20-35% alpha) over a sky-blue/green gradient, radius 12-16px, thin light border, top-edge specular highlight.
donts: Don't fake the style with fuzzy drop shadows — its depth language is gloss and translucency; avoid for serious enterprise and data tools where gloss undermines credibility and costs rendering performance.

characteristics: Digital surfaces that feel tangible via material cues — warm material tones, subtle grain, dimensional lighting — without 2010-era literal leather-and-felt metaphors.
dos: Use warm material tones (never pure #fff/#000); subtle noise texture at 0.04-0.06 opacity; layered shadow stack implying a single top light source; letterpress/inset text for engraved labels; strongest in AR/VR, smart-home controls, and onboarding for non-technical users. Card chrome: warm material surface, radius 8-12px, layered soft shadow implying one top light source, 1px slightly-darker border.
donts: Don't push noise above ~0.1 opacity (reads as dirt); don't mix light-source directions across components; avoid on dense dashboards where texture competes with data.

characteristics: Extruded-from-the-surface look: element fill equals page background, dual light+dark shadows imply molded hardware. Peaked 2020; near-zero production use today.
dos: If used at all: resting state -8px -8px 16px light plus 8px 8px 16px dark, pressed state same values inset; radius 12-20px; dark mode uses tinted highlight/shade never pure white/black; push text to 7:1, add accent borders to interactive elements, explicit focus-visible rings.
donts: Canonical recipe fails accessibility by the numbers: edge contrast ~1.4:1 versus the 3:1 WCAG non-text minimum, and interactive surfaces are indistinguishable from static ones. Never use for accessibility-critical, trust-critical, or data-dense products; treat as novelty-widget territory only.

characteristics: Synthetic efficiency juxtaposed with natural elements — water, greenery, organic curves against digital motifs — for an approachable, dreamlike tech environment.
dos: Integrate nature imagery or organic forms with digital UI motifs; use high-saturation blue-green palettes or pastel aqua with soft shadows for a breezy quality; let organic shapes soften geometric layouts.
donts: Don't let decoration bury function — organic elements frame content, not replace hierarchy; avoid when the brand voice is precision/instrument rather than warmth.

characteristics: Asymmetric grid of rounded modules (bento-box metaphor) organizing mixed content sizes into one composed view. Current mainstream (Apple, Linear, 2026 SaaS landing pages).
dos: Use CSS Grid with deliberate module-size variation; gutters 16-24px; radius 16-32px; cap hero tiles at 2 per screen; give each module one clear content job; let cell size encode importance. Card chrome per module: filled surface with subtle contrast against the page background, radius 16-24px, hairline or no shadow.
donts: Don't fill a bento with equal-size cells (defeats the hierarchy purpose); don't exceed 2 hero tiles; don't force unrelated content into one module to fill space.

characteristics: Oversized neo-grotesque or geometric display type as the primary interface architecture — type is the layout. Reaction against homogenized minimal SaaS aesthetics.
dos: Let one oversized display face (e.g. Syne, Space Grotesk class) carry the visual identity; keep body text deliberately plain; combine with raw borders and flat blocks; suits portfolios, editorial, indie brands.
donts: Don't pair two loud display faces; don't apply to banking/healthcare/regulated domains; oversized type still needs a responsive minimum — test wrapping at small breakpoints.

characteristics: Ambient light as atmosphere: smoky, grainy, multi-hue aurora gradients and soft glow used as lighting, not decoration. Part of the calm-interface pushback against overstimulation.
dos: Use soft multi-hue gradients as background lighting with visible grain to avoid banding; pastel blue/green glow for cozy night-light moods, paired with bokeh or soft shadows; keep foreground UI crisp against the atmospheric layer.
donts: Don't stack neon or oversaturated glows (generative-AI tell); don't let gradient atmosphere reduce text contrast below WCAG; don't use gradient-tinted text for body copy.

characteristics: An image means something only when form (how it is made), content (what is shown), and context (where and next to what it appears) are designed together.
dos: When constructing or selecting imagery, articulate all three: the formal treatment, the subject, and the placement context; reject imagery where any one is arbitrary; use the equation as the acceptance test for hero images and campaign photography.
donts: Don't select images on form alone (pretty but meaningless) or content alone (correct but flat); don't ignore context — the same photo reads differently beside different neighbors.

characteristics: High-contrast single-source lighting compresses space, emphasizes tactile texture, and creates narrative tension by pulling the eye to a localized focal area.
dos: Use a single directional key light at ~45 degrees with deep shadow falloff; minimize fill light; let pitch-black negative space frame the subject; emphasize localized texture.
donts: Don't add fill that flattens the drama; don't use for products needing an open, airy, trustworthy feel; watch that shadow detail survives compression on dark-mode displays.

characteristics: Subject isolation via lighting ratio: background lit separately and brighter than the key light eliminates background shadows entirely.
dos: Light the background independently, about 2 stops brighter than the key (4:1 illuminance); use multiple strobes with V-flats; ideal for clean e-commerce and product photography.
donts: Don't rely on post-processing cutouts to fake it — edge light contamination shows; don't blow highlights past recoverable range.

characteristics: Meaning is defined by the exact instant of capture — the frame where gesture, event, and composition align (Cartier-Bresson). Applies to photo selection and to timing screenshots of product moments.
dos: Choose or capture frames at the peak instant (mid-air, mid-gesture, the moment of alignment); account for shutter/device latency; in product imagery, show the moment of value delivery, not the aftermath.
donts: Don't settle for the frame just before or after the peak; don't stage stiff poses when the story is motion.

characteristics: Whose gaze the viewer follows dictates the power structure of a portrait; subjects reading as active agents (not passive specimens) carry dignity and story.
dos: Identify whose gaze the composition privileges; direct eye-line and posture to signal agency; let subjects participate in shaping the visual story; treat concept and aesthetics as inseparable.
donts: Don't compose portraits where the subject is a passive object of observation unless that power reading is intentional; don't crop in ways that strip agency.

characteristics: Placing a subject within their territory — workplace, landscape, community — anchors identity and tells a larger story than an isolated portrait.
dos: Capture subjects within environments that represent their bonds and identity; use wide depth of field so the territory stays sharp while the subject remains central.
donts: Don't default to seamless-backdrop isolation when identity and place are the story; don't blur context into abstraction if it carries meaning.

characteristics: A small subject against a vast environment makes the environment the true subject and rewards closer viewing — scale contrast as narrative.
dos: Use a small figure or object as the reference point that reveals the scale of the surrounding scene; compose so the image reads first as landscape, then as story on inspection.
donts: Don't center-blow-up the subject when the scale relationship is the point; don't clutter the frame so scale contrast is lost.

principle: Sequencing Logic (images speak to each other)
characteristics: Adjacent images create meaning through proximity and order — a person fishing next to a fish stall reads as cause and effect. Image sequences are edited narratives.
dos: Sequence and place imagery deliberately: pairs and runs should build cause-effect or thematic rhythm; in layouts, treat neighboring images as one composition; storyboard galleries before filling them.
donts: Don't shuffle imagery as interchangeable decoration; don't place images adjacently whose accidental juxtaposition creates unintended readings.

characteristics: Ultra-slow shutter speeds simplify moving subjects into pure tonality — silky water, silk-like forms, low-saturation calm. Abstraction through time.
dos: Use >= 10s exposures with ND filters to render motion as smooth tonal fields; favor low-saturation pastel palettes; use for landscape and mood imagery where serenity is the message.
donts: Don't mix frozen-action subjects into a meditative long-exposure set; don't oversaturate — the register is calm.

characteristics: Color defines the structure and atmosphere of a world — signifying internal states, social meaning, and coherence — rather than decorating it.
dos: Build imagery palettes that construct the world: mist, artificial light, and architectural lines as coherent atmosphere; use color to signal internal states or social message; keep one photographic tension per palette.
donts: Don't apply color grading as arbitrary decoration; don't mix atmosphere palettes within one narrative sequence without a reason.

characteristics: Characters built from basic primitives (circles, rectangles, rounded torsos, dot eyes, single-curve mouths) remove individual identity to foreground collective, universal interaction.
dos: Use primitive-based construction with rounded corners for softness; minimal facial mapping (two dots, one curve); suits diagrams, empty states, and community-level storytelling where any-person universality helps.
donts: Don't use faceless abstraction where individual identity, diversity, or emotional nuance is the message; see Corporate Memphis caveats before adopting wholesale.

characteristics: Showing the actual product interface in marketing imagery communicates function better than abstract metaphor illustration.
dos: Replace abstract metaphors with grounded imagery of the product in action: real screenshots, real components as graphic elements, real use cases; keep shown UI current with the shipped product.
donts: Don't fabricate fake product screenshots from styled divs and present them as real; don't let marketing UI drift from the actual product (trust damage on arrival).

characteristics: UX as staged choreography: interactions are a planned sequence of movements that reveal position in a digital space and build narrative meaning — a dance between user and interface.
dos: Arrange interaction steps in a deliberate sequence toward task completion; define keyframe intervals and movement paths; use proximity so single steps read as part of a group; storyboard multi-step motion before building.
donts: Don't animate steps in isolation without a sequence logic; don't choreograph decoration that hides where the user is in the flow.

characteristics: Scrollytelling: pinning and scrubbing elements synchronized to scroll position turns a page into a paced, chaptered story.
dos: Pin key scenes and scrub their animation to scroll progress; chapter the narrative so each pinned section makes one point; keep scrub animations on composited properties for smoothness; provide a reduced-motion path that preserves content order.
donts: Don't hijack scroll speed or reverse scroll direction; don't pin so long that users feel trapped; don't gate core content behind scroll theatrics.

characteristics: Fluid, organic movement — buoyant forms, water-like response to input — reduces perceived coldness of technology and suits nature-tech and wellness aesthetics.
dos: Use ease-in-out curves that mimic buoyancy; let decorative forms (bubbles, blobs, gradients) respond subtly to pointer or scroll input; pair with techno-organic or atmospheric styles.
donts: Don't apply fluid physics to functional UI elements where responsiveness must feel instant; keep particle/mesh effects within the performance budget and honor prefers-reduced-motion.

characteristics: Soft 3D clay look: big radii, dual inner shadows plus tinted outer shadow, pastel matte surfaces. Coined 2021 (Malewicz) as the accessible fix for neumorphism; by 2026 niche-settled, not novel.
dos: Use border-radius 20-40px; triple shadow stack (large soft outer drop tinted to surface hue, inset bottom-right shade, inset top-left highlight); pastel palette (lavender, mint, peach, baby blue) with matte finish; strongest for onboarding flows, kids' apps, friendly-face fintech, 3D landing pages.
donts: Avoid for developer tools, luxury, government, and editorial/news; re-check contrast per instance — pastel-on-pastel with soft shadows can still fail WCAG even though the style was born as an accessibility fix.

characteristics: Chrome, gradient mesh, iridescence, pixel/dither texture — the 2025-26 wave is material-driven and systemic (chrome with weight and behavior), not the 2021 surface-level kitsch. Functions partly as an anti-AI-slop authenticity signal for Gen-Z audiences.
dos: Use metallic/chrome effects and holographic highlights over silver base; hot pink and electric blue primaries, lime accents, violet depth; pixel/dither as deliberate texture; commit systemically (motion, texture, material logic), not as a pasted filter; fits gaming, fan communities, Gen-Z consumer brands.
donts: Don't use as decoration without systemic commitment — reads shallow and dated; avoid for fintech, healthcare, government, luxury (breaks trust or restraint signals); time-boxed nostalgia cycle — re-verify currency before recommending as a durable identity.

characteristics: Density with structure: one expressive display typeface at large scale, dense layered grid, oversized headlines — typography/grid-led maximalism, distinct from ornament-led decoration. Market driver is minimalism fatigue.
dos: Use ONE dominant bold display face at hero scale (not three competing fonts); keep the grid disciplined under the density; layer imagery and texture with intentional hierarchy; fits news/editorial, publishing, and brands differentiating from muted minimalist sameness.
donts: Without a single dominant typeface and real grid discipline it collapses into visual noise; avoid for government, healthcare, and data-dense product UI; reactive/cyclical trend — moderate durability confidence.
